list.listitem: Retinoblastoma is a childhood intraocular cancer caused by the defect or absence of a tumor suppressor gene; retinoblastoma may be familial or sporadic. C
Children with a family history should undergo ophthalmic screening from birth until 4 years of age. B
Sporadic retinoblastoma is associated with increasing paternal age, poor maternal diet, and in vitro fertilization. B

Chemoreduction with adjuvant focal therapy has become a first-line treatment for intraocular retinoblastoma, with many sites using intra-arterial chemotherapy despite a lack of high quality evidence. B
If the tumor is confined to the eye, childhood survival is 95%. B
Lifetime risk of a second nonocular cancer is about 35%. Second nonocular cancers are the most significant cause of morbidity and mortality in familial retinoblastoma. B

background.definition: Retinoblastoma is an eye cancer of childhood that occurs in the developing retinal cell or retinoblast. There are 2 forms: familial retinoblastoma, due to a new or inherited germline RB1 mutation or deletion, and sporadic retinoblastoma, due to both somatic RB1 mutations and deletions occurring in a retinoblast. Trilateral retinoblastoma (TRB) is the association of familial retinoblastoma with a midline intracranial neuroblastic tumor.

list.listitem: Retinoblastoma occurs in 1 in 20,000 live births, of which 40% are familial and 60% are sporadic.
There are 200 to 250 new cases each year in the United States.
About 8% of cases with familial retinoblastoma develop TRB.
Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy of childhood.
RB1 gene (Ch 13q14) mutation or deletion
13q deletion syndrome
RB1 mutation and p53 deletion in synergism for the development of retinoblastoma

The RB1 gene is a tumor suppressor gene. Germline mutations show autosomal dominant inheritance or occur in early embryogenesis, usually in the paternal chromosome. Ninety percent of children with the germline mutation will develop retinoblastoma. This is known as familial retinoblastoma.

Knudson 2-hit hypothesis: both copies of the gene must be mutated or deleted ("hits") for retinoblastoma to occur. In familial retinoblastoma the "first hit" is already present. A spontaneous mutation, "second hit, " has to occur in the remaining normal RB1 gene for retinoblastoma to develop. As the first hit is present in every cell, familial retinoblastoma tends to be multifocal, is often bilateral (85%), and carries the risk of second nonocular cancers and TRB.

In sporadic retinoblastoma, both first and second hits have to occur in the same developing retinal cell. Hence sporadic retinoblastoma is always unifocal, unilateral, and carries no risk of second cancers.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Maternal diet lacking in fruits and vegetables

list.listitem: Although widely recommended, red reflex testing is not an effective screening method for retinoblastoma. C
Screening for the RB1 mutation is cost effective in determining which family members should undergo screening.
Children at risk of hereditary retinoblastoma should undergo regular ophthalmic screening by an ophthalmologist from birth until the age of 4. B

Consider MRI of the brain, performed every 6 months, for the first 5 years of life to detect TRB in those with familial disease. Screening results in earlier detection of TRB, but age at death is unaffected. Early detection may result in a higher cure rate for trilateral TRB. C
Dilated fundus examination of both eyes with the indirect ophthalmoscope must be performed by a pediatric ocular oncologist. C
Ocular ultrasound is helpful in identifying a retinal mass. Foci of calcification make the diagnosis of retinoblastoma very likely. C
Identification of the germline RB1 mutation determines the definitive diagnosis of familial retinoblastoma. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Peripheral retinal telangiectasia with yellow retinal exudation
Microphthalmos, retrolental mass, prominent ciliary processes
Cystic tumor, anterior location, lens coloboma

list.listitem: Children diagnosed in the first year of life usually have bilateral disease.
The majority of children present with leukocoria detected by a family member. Loss of the red reflex is subsequently identified in early photographs.
It is important to take a complete family history.
An ophthalmologist should perform a dilated fundus examination of the parents and siblings to look for the presence of a treated retinoblastoma or an undiagnosed retinocytoma/retinoma.

The diagnosis of retinoblastoma is made by a dilated fundus examination of both eyes under general anesthesia. The retina is examined with an indirect ophthalmoscope and scleral indentation is performed to visualize the peripheral retina. A and B scan ocular ultrasonography is used to confirm the presence of a retinal mass containing foci of calcification. Retcam images are often used to stage and monitor disease.
Systemic pediatric evaluation is performed to identify features of the 13q deletion syndrome.
MRI should be performed if optic nerve or orbital invasion is suspected. MRI can also be used in familial disease to identify TRB.

Peripheral blood should be tested for the germline RB1 mutation in all affected children. The DNA of the affected children can be compared with standard probes if the mutation in that family has been identified. Alternatively, following enucleation, DNA analysis is performed on fresh tumor tissue, which is compared with the DNA of peripheral blood leukocytes in the same patient.

If toxocariasis is suspected, inquire about a history of contact with puppies. ELISA serology for toxocara is positive in 90% of patients with toxocariasis and up to 23% of normal healthy preschool children.
If metastatic disease is suspected, patients should undergo bone marrow biopsy and lumbar puncture to stage the disease.
See attached algorithm.
Chemoreduction with adjuvant focal therapy is the recommended first-line treatment for intraocular retinoblastoma. B
Primary enucleation may still be necessary for advanced unilateral disease. B
Local chemotherapy may be beneficial for advanced disease with vitreous seeds. C
Metastatic disease is treated with aggressive chemotherapy and stem cell rescue. C
Chemoreduction is the use of systemic primary chemotherapy to shrink the tumor.
Various chemotherapy regimens include: carboplatin alone; vincristine and carboplatin; vincristine etoposide and carboplatin; vincristine, etoposide, carboplatin, and cyclosporin.

Local chemotherapy, such as subtenon injection of carboplatin, is used as adjuvant focal treatment. In some centers, intra-arterial and intravitreal melphalan is used for eyes that would otherwise be removed (group E) and for extensive vitreous seeds. Local delivery devices are still experimental.

Treatment of retinoblastoma varies widely around the world. Chemotherapy regimens include different reagents, treatment doses, and number of cycles. Not all centers have published their results. Most current evidence is based on systemic treatment with 6 cycles of vincristine, etoposide, and carboplatin with or without cyclosporin. Few studies have investigated the additional benefits of multiple consolidation treatments.

In a trial with 187 patients use of 3 cycles of post-resection chemotherapy (carboplatin,etoposide, vincristine) had non-inferior 5 year disease free survival compared to the full 6 cycles of chemotherapy.

A recent innovation in the management of retinoblastoma has been the use of intra- ophthalmic artery chemotherapy (mephalan) in treatment of advance disease (stage D/E). The femoral artery is catheterized and the ophthalmic artery is accessed via the carotid artery using a microcatheter. This avoids the systemic side effects of chemotherapy in these very young children, and there is some suggestion that it may deliver better visual outcomes and ocular survival than intravenous chemotherapy. The treatment is only used in selected cases as it is not yet widely accepted as first line therapy, and has not been studied in RCTs. A recent meta-analysis of intra-arterial hemotherapy was unable to conclude there was benefit and further research is required.

The Children's Oncology Group (COG, USA) has initiated four trials to provide evidence for the treatment of retinoblastoma. COG will investigate the need for adjuvant chemotherapy in enucleated patients with high-risk histology. Group B eyes will be treated with vincristine and carboplatin plus consolidation. Group C/D eyes will receive high-dose triple-agent chemotherapy plus orbital floor carboplatin. The COG trials will also investigate the success of chemotherapy for metastatic disease.

Adjuvant focal therapy is applied at the time of chemotherapy (consolidation treatment) or following completion of chemotherapy. Methods of adjuvant focal therapy include: diode laser thermotherapy; chemothermotherapy; cryotherapy; argon laser photocoagulation; brachytherapy (episcleral plaque radiotherapy); subtenon carboplatin injection. An Cochrane review into the efficacy of laser therapy as adjuvant with systemic chemotherapy found no clinical trials to address this question.

Salvage treatment is used for recurrence or failure of primary chemotherapy/chemoreduction and adjuvant focal treatment. Methods of salvage treatment include: diode laser thermotherapy; chemothermotherapy; cryotherapy; brachytherapy (episcleral plaque radiotherapy); external beam radiotherapy; local chemotherapy.
Primary enucleation is the surgical removal of an eye. Secondary enucleation is the surgical removal of an eye that has failed chemoreduction with adjuvant focal therapy and salvage treatment.
Exenteration is the removal of the eye and the orbital contents. Exenteration is reserved for orbital disease.
Hospitalization is required to site a central venous line under general anaesthesia for the administration of chemotherapy. Chemotherapy can be administered as a day case procedure.
Chemotherapy is delivered for a total of six cycles at 3 to 4 week intervals. Patients are monitored for bone marrow suppression.

Event-free survival following chemoreduction and adjuvant focal treatment depends on the international classification group for retinoblastoma: 100% group A; 93% group B; 90% group C; 47% group D. Group E eyes undergo enucleation. B

Childhood survival depends on the stage at diagnosis, with 95% childhood survival for intraocular disease, 40% survival for orbital disease, 20% for distal metastases, and 1% to 5% for intracranial disease. B
Childhood survival for TRB depends on tumor size. Cumulative 5-year survivals are 24% for TRB <15 mm and 0% for TRB >15 mm. A
Chemoreduction may protect against TRB. B
Circulating tumor DNA following treatment does correlate with clinical outcome.

Lifetime risk of a second nonocular malignancy in familial retinoblastoma is about 35%, with a relative risk of 13.4 compared with normal controls. The common malignancies are osteosarcoma, soft tissue sarcoma, and melanoma. Low-dose diagnostic radiation, including CT scans and therapeutic radiotherapy, increase the risk of second cancers.
Excessive sunbathing should be avoided.

A retinocytoma/retinoma is a benign retinal tumor that resembles a treated retinoblastoma. If a retinocytoma/retinoma is found in the relative of an affected child, then this implies that the condition is familial.
Retinoblastoma is rare in adulthood but is usually due to malignant transformation of a retinocytoma/retinoma. Adults with retinocytoma/retinoma should be monitored for life.
Lifetime risk of a second nonocular malignancy in familial retinoblastoma is about 35% (most often osteosarcoma, soft tissue sarcoma, and melanoma).
Prenatal genetic diagnosis for familial retinoblastoma is an option.

Prenatal ultrasound during the third trimester may detect retinoblastoma in the developing fetus and allow early delivery; however, the risks and benefits of early induction and then chemotherapy in a premature baby should be considered.
Couples with a family history of retinoblastoma who are planning a family but are concerned about the risk of retinoblastoma should undergo genetic counseling.
